title: 23. Backgrounding strategy impacts finishing performance and carcass characteristics.
content:
Abstract
Backgrounding, the post-weaning phase preceding finishing, establishes the physiological foundation for subsequent feedlot performance and carcass development. Management and nutritional strategies employed during backgrounding exert lasting effects on growth efficiency, finishing performance, and carcass merit. Key backgrounding factors influencing subsequent performance include the rate of gain during the growing phase, the type of backgrounding system (dry-lot vs. stocker grazing), and body composition at feedyard entry. Many cattle managers rely on compensatory gain when making purchasing and management decisions during finishing. Although compensatory growth can occur following periods of restricted gain, responses are highly variable, often transient, and generally insufficient to fully offset differences in body weight at the start of the finishing period. To further evaluate how backgrounding nutrition influences subsequent finishing performance and carcass characteristics, treatment means from 40 experiments were compiled in which cattle were finished following backgrounding under a wide range of environments and pre-finishing performance levels. Data were analyzed using mixed models with study included as a random effect, and analyses were conducted separately for dry-lot and stocker backgrounding systems. Growing-phase average daily gain (ADG) was included as a continuous fixed effect, and responses were adjusted to a common degree of finish by centering 12th-rib backfat thickness at 1.524 cm. Denominator degrees of freedom were estimated using the Kenward–Roger method. In dry-lot backgrounding systems, body weight at harvest increased (P < 0.01) by approximately 21 kg for each 1-kg increase in backgrounding ADG. In contrast, cattle backgrounded in stocker grazing systems tended (P = 0.06) to increase harvest body weight by 13.7 kg per 1-kg increase in growing-phase ADG. For both backgrounding systems, finishing ADG declined as backgrounding ADG increased (P < 0.01), however, the negative effect of increased backgrounding ADG on finishing performance was 76% greater in dry-lot systems than in stocker grazing systems. Feed efficiency (feed:gain) was negatively affected by increasing backgrounding ADG in dry-lot programs (P < 0.01) but was not significantly impacted in stocker systems (P = 0.14). Days on feed decreased with increasing backgrounding ADG in stocker systems (P < 0.01) but were not affected in dry-lot programs (P = 0.26). Hot carcass weight was positively influenced by backgrounding ADG in both systems. However, ribeye area and carcass quality traits were affected by backgrounding performance only in stocker grazing systems (P ≤ 0.05) and not in dry-lot programs (P ≥ 0.15). Increasing performance during dry-lot backgrounding has greater negative consequences for finishing performance and efficiency and exerts less influence on carcass quality compared with increasing performance during forage-based stocker grazing. Additional research is needed to directly compare body composition changes during dry-lot and stocker backgrounding and to clarify how these differences influence finishing performance, efficiency, and carcass merit.
